questions.q: In the context of concrete as an 'artificial stone,' which specific mix ratio is designated as Class AA, typically used for underwater or high-strength applications?
questions.n: Class AA is the richest standard mix, providing high density and strength for specialized structural needs.

questions.q: Which type of admixture is specifically used to increase the rate of hydration, thereby shortening the setting time and increasing the rate of strength gain?
o: Plasticizer
Retarder
Accelerator
Air-entraining agent
questions.n: Accelerators are often used in cold weather to speed up the curing process and allow for earlier formwork removal.

questions.q: According to standard practice, what is the maximum allowable slump for Reinforced Concrete (RC) Beams and Columns?
o: 25 mm (1 inch)
100 mm (4 inches)
50 mm (2 inches)
150 mm (6 inches)
questions.n: This slump provides the necessary workability to flow around dense rebar while maintaining structural integrity.

questions.q: When performing a slump test, what are the standard dimensions (Top Diameter x Height x Bottom Diameter) of the slump cone?
o: 150 mm x 300 mm x 150 mm
102 mm x 305 mm x 203 mm
203 mm x 203 mm x 305 mm
100 mm x 200 mm x 100 mm
questions.n: These dimensions (4" x 12" x 8") are the industry standard defined by ACI and ASTM for testing concrete consistency.

questions.q: What percentage of the design compressive strength is concrete typically expected to reach after the first week (7 days) of curing?
questions.n: Reaching approximately 70% at 7 days is a standard benchmark used to determine if concrete is on track for its 28-day target.

questions.q: A 'Prescribed Mixture' differs from a 'Designed Mixture' in that:
o: It requires laboratory testing to determine the best water-cement ratio.
It is only used for high-rise buildings.
The proportions are dictated by the specifier, rather than the desired performance.
The contractor chooses the proportions based on local experience.
questions.n: In a prescribed mix, the specific amounts of cement, water, and aggregate are mandated regardless of the resulting strength.

questions.q: Which piece of equipment is used to transport concrete from the truck to high or hard-to-reach areas of a structure using a flexible arm?
o: Line Pump
Boom Pump
Agitator Truck
Bagger Mixer
questions.n: Boom pumps use a remote-controlled robotic arm (boom) to place concrete precisely over obstacles and at height.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between Air-Entrained and Non-Air Entrained concrete?
o: Air-entrained concrete is heavier.
Non-air entrained concrete is easier to work with.
Air-entrained concrete contains billions of microscopic bubbles to improve durability.
Non-air entrained concrete has better resistance to freeze-thaw cycles.
questions.n: These bubbles act as relief valves for internal pressure when water inside the concrete freezes.

questions.q: For 'Mass Concrete' such as large dams or heavy mat foundations, what is the generally recommended maximum slump?
o: 25 mm to 50 mm (1 to 2 inches)
No slump (0 mm)
125 mm to 150 mm (5 to 6 inches)
75 mm to 100 mm (3 to 4 inches)
questions.n: Mass concrete requires very little water to reduce heat of hydration and potential cracking.

questions.q: In construction specifications, what does the 'ACI' stand for when referring to concrete standards?
o: Associated Cement Industries
Architectural Concrete Institute
American Concrete Institute
American Construction International
questions.n: The ACI is the primary authority for concrete design, construction, and materials standards in the US and many other regions.

questions.q: Which concrete mix ratio is standard for Class B concrete, typically utilized for footings and foundation walls?
questions.n: Class B is a leaner mix than Class A, making it economical and sufficient for non-critical structural footings.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a 'Retarder' admixture in a concrete mix?
o: To increase the early strength of the concrete.
To reduce the amount of water required for workability.
To prevent the concrete from freezing in cold climates.
To delay the initial set of concrete, especially in hot weather.
questions.n: Retarders slow down the chemical reaction of hydration, preventing the concrete from hardening too quickly during transport or placement.

questions.q: In the classification of sand for concrete, what is 'S1' sand primarily used for?
o: Filling and sub-base preparation.
As a substitute for coarse aggregate.
Plastering and fine finishing work.
Structural concrete and heavy foundations.
questions.n: S1 refers to the finest grade of sand, which provides the smooth texture required for interior and exterior plaster.

questions.q: For a massive structural member like a footing, what is the minimum recommended curing period before removing the formwork side-supports?
o: 28 days
7 days
14 days
24 to 48 hours
questions.n: Since footings are supported by the ground, the side forms can be removed relatively early once the concrete has reached initial set.

questions.q: Which ready-mix concrete delivery method is best suited for residential projects with narrow access where a large boom cannot reach?
o: Boom Pump
Line Pump
Agitator Truck alone
Bagger Mixer
questions.n: Line pumps use flexible hoses that can be snaked through houses or narrow alleys to reach the pour site.

questions.q: What is the standard allowable slump range for concrete used in Pavements and Slabs?
o: 100 mm to 150 mm (4 to 6 inches)
50 mm to 100 mm (2 to 4 inches)
25 mm to 75 mm (1 to 3 inches)
150 mm to 200 mm (6 to 8 inches)
questions.n: Slabs and pavements require a stiffer mix to ensure the surface can be finished properly without excessive bleeding.

questions.q: Which structural element typically requires the longest curing time and support (shoring) before the formwork is fully removed?
o: Cantilever Beams
Columns
Wall side forms
Footings
questions.n: Cantilevers are entirely dependent on the strength of the concrete at the support point and require maximum curing time to avoid deflection.

questions.q: When referring to aggregates, 'Fine Aggregate' is defined as material that can pass through which sieve size?
o: No. 4 Sieve (4.75 mm)
3/4 inch Sieve
No. 10 Sieve
No. 200 Sieve
questions.n: Aggregate passing the No. 4 sieve is classified as sand or fine aggregate; anything retained is coarse aggregate.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of using 'Non-Air Entrained' concrete in environments subject to severe freeze-thaw cycles?
o: The concrete will become too heavy.
The concrete will set too slowly.
Internal pressure from freezing water will cause surface scaling and 'pop-outs'.
The mix will be too difficult to pump.
questions.n: Without the relief valves provided by air bubbles, the expansion of freezing water ruptures the concrete paste.

questions.q: In a standard 'Designed Mixture,' who is responsible for determining the exact proportions of the concrete constituents?
o: The Architect
The Concrete Lab/Supplier
The Mason on site
The Building Inspector
questions.n: In a designed mix, the supplier performs trials to ensure the mix meets the engineer's strength and durability requirements.

questions.q: What is the maximum allowable slump for concrete footings, caissons, and substructure walls?
o: 150 mm (6 inches)
25 mm (1 inch)
75 mm (3 inches)
125 mm (5 inches)
questions.n: These below-grade elements need to be sturdy and are usually less congested with rebar than upper-level beams.

questions.q: Plasticizers (Water Reducers) are added to a concrete mix primarily to:
o: Change the color of the concrete.
Shorten the curing time to 24 hours.
Increase workability without increasing the water-cement ratio.
Make the concrete waterproof.
questions.n: This allows for a fluid, easy-to-pour mix while maintaining the high strength associated with low water content.

questions.q: A concrete mix with a 1 : 3 : 6 ratio (Class C) is most appropriate for which of the following?
o: Multi-story building columns.
Suspended floor slabs.
Pre-stressed concrete beams.
Plant boxes and non-load bearing path-walks.
questions.n: Class C is a lean mix used for decorative or non-structural elements where strength is not a primary concern.

questions.q: What is the typical ratio of 'Fine Aggregate' to 'Coarse Aggregate' in a standard Class A (1 : 2 : 4) mix?
o: 1 part sand to 4 parts gravel
2 parts sand to 1 part gravel
1 part sand to 1 part gravel
1 part sand to 2 parts gravel
questions.n: In the 1:2:4 ratio, '2' represents the sand (fine) and '4' represents the gravel (coarse), creating a 1:2 relationship.

questions.q: Which type of concrete mixer is commonly seen on small construction sites and involves manual loading of 'bags' of cement?
o: Batch Plant
Transit Mixer
Agitator Truck
Bagger Mixer
questions.n: Also known as a drum mixer, it is sized to handle specific numbers of cement bags per batch.

questions.q: For 'Substructure Walls' that are reinforced, what is the maximum allowable slump?
o: 25 mm (1 inch)
50 mm (2 inches)
175 mm (7 inches)
100 mm (4 inches)
questions.n: Reinforced walls require a bit more workability (4 inches) compared to mass concrete to ensure the mix flows around the rebar.

questions.q: What is the typical curing period required for concrete 'Columns' before they are considered strong enough to have their vertical forms removed?
o: 12 hours
2 to 5 days
21 days
14 days
questions.n: Columns gain strength quickly enough that their side-forms can be removed early, provided they aren't yet taking significant floor loads.

questions.q: Which sand classification is slightly coarser than plastering sand and is suitable for general masonry work and mortar?
o: Gravel
S1
Silt
S2
questions.n: S2 is a medium-grade sand, ideal for laying bricks/blocks and general concrete work.

questions.q: What term describes the ease with which a freshly mixed concrete can be transported, placed, consolidated, and finished?
o: Workability
Durability
Plasticity
Consistency
questions.n: Workability is a broad term encompassing all aspects of how easy the concrete is to handle on-site.

questions.q: Concrete is often referred to as 'Artificial Stone' because:
o: It hardens through a chemical process into a rock-like mass.
It is just as expensive as natural marble.
It is mined directly from the earth like granite.
It can only be used to make statues.
questions.n: The hydration of cement binds aggregates together to create a material with properties similar to natural conglomerate rock.

questions.q: For a massive concrete footing, why is the side formwork typically allowed to be removed within 24 to 48 hours?
o: The concrete reaches 70% strength within the first 48 hours.
The earth provides lateral support, and the forms are not carrying vertical loads.
The slump is high enough to allow quick setting.
Massive footings use higher cement content (Class AA).
questions.n: Side forms for ground-supported elements only maintain shape, not structural integrity, allowing for early stripping.

questions.q: In a situation where concrete must be placed in a deep, narrow trench with high rebar density, which delivery system is most efficient?
o: Agitator Truck chute
Line Pump
Bagger Mixer
Wheelbarrow
questions.n: A line pump allows for steady, controlled placement via a flexible hose, which is ideal for navigating congested reinforcement.

questions.q: What is the industry-standard maximum slump for concrete used in reinforced foundation walls and footings?
o: 75 mm (3 inches)
25 mm (1 inch)
125 mm (5 inches)
150 mm (6 inches)
questions.n: A 3-inch slump provides the necessary balance between placement ease and structural density for footings.

questions.q: In the standard Class A mix (1 : 2 : 4), what does the number '4' represent?
o: The parts of Cement.
The parts of Coarse Aggregate.
The parts of Water.
The parts of Fine Aggregate.
questions.n: The standard ratio follows the order: Cement : Sand (Fine) : Gravel (Coarse).

questions.q: For 'Pavements and Slabs' on grade, why is the allowable slump capped at 75 mm (3 inches)?
o: To reduce surface bleeding and ensure a durable finish.
To prevent the slab from cracking under its own weight.
To increase the heat of hydration.
To make it easier for the pump to move the concrete.
questions.n: Lower water content (lower slump) prevents excess water from rising to the surface, which would weaken the wear layer.

questions.q: Which specific admixture is used when concrete must be transported over very long distances or poured in extremely high temperatures?
o: Accelerator
Air-entraining agent
Plasticizer
Retarder
questions.n: Retarders extend the 'open time' of the mix, keeping it workable despite heat or long transit times.

questions.q: When casting a cantilevered balcony, when is it generally safe to remove the supporting shores (soffit forms)?
o: Once the columns are poured.
After 48 hours.
After 7 days.
When the concrete reaches full design strength, usually 28 days.
questions.n: Cantilevers are high-risk members; stripping too early can cause immediate structural failure or excessive deflection.

questions.q: What is the primary benefit of using 'S2' sand over 'S1' sand in a concrete mix?
o: It makes the concrete waterproof.
It is easier to pump through a line pump.
It provides a smoother finish for plastering.
It requires less cement to coat the particles, making the mix more economical.
questions.n: Coarser sand (S2) has less total surface area than fine sand (S1), requiring less cement paste to bind.

questions.q: Which of the following describes 'Workability' in a way that distinguishes it from 'Slump'?
o: Workability is a measure of the concrete's final compressive strength.
Workability is the measure of concrete height after the cone is removed.
Workability is only relevant for air-entrained concrete.
Workability includes the ease of consolidation and the ability to resist segregation.
questions.n: While slump measures fluidness, workability is a qualitative measure of how easily the concrete is placed and finished.

questions.q: What is the standard height of an ACI-compliant slump cone?
o: 150 mm (6 inches)
203 mm (8 inches)
305 mm (12 inches)
102 mm (4 inches)
questions.n: The standard slump cone is 12 inches high, with a 4-inch top and 8-inch base.

questions.q: Why is 'Class AA' concrete (1 : 1.5 : 3) specified for underwater pours?
o: It is cheaper to produce in large volumes.
It doesn't require aggregates.
The higher cement content ensures the mix remains cohesive and resists washout from water.
It is lighter and floats better during the pour.
questions.n: A richer mix (more cement) creates a stickier, denser concrete that is less likely to separate when in contact with water.

questions.q: If a concrete cylinder reaches 70% of its strength at 7 days, is the mix design considered successful?
o: No, it must reach 100% at 7 days.
Yes, this follows the standard curve for strength gain.
No, 70% is too low; it should be at 90%.
Yes, but only if an accelerator was used.
questions.n: The 7-day test is a reliable indicator that the concrete will meet its full design strength by 28 days.

questions.q: What is the primary visual difference between a 'Line Pump' and a 'Boom Pump' on a construction site?
o: The Boom Pump doesn't use a truck.
The Line Pump is mounted on a separate truck.
The Boom Pump has a hydraulic folding arm; the Line Pump uses manual hoses.
The Line Pump is much larger.
questions.n: A boom pump allows for overhead placement, while a line pump requires workers to pull hoses across the ground.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key characteristic of 'Non-Air Entrained' concrete?
o: It is always used for underwater construction.
It uses more sand than air-entrained concrete.
It has a lower percentage of 'voids' or air pockets within the mix.
It is highly resistant to freezing.
questions.n: Non-air entrained concrete only contains 'entrapped' air from mixing, which is generally less than 1-2%.

questions.q: When casting 'Columns' and 'Beams' simultaneously, why is a slump of 100 mm (4 inches) often allowed?
o: To reduce the amount of vibration needed.
To make the concrete dry faster.
Because columns are not structural.
To allow the concrete to flow into small spaces around dense rebar.
questions.n: Vertical members and beams have congested steel; the concrete needs enough 'flow' (4-inch slump) to avoid honeycombing.

questions.q: What is the main function of an 'Agitator Truck' during transport?
o: To pump the concrete to the 10th floor.
To measure the exact volume being poured.
To heat the concrete during winter.
To keep the concrete in motion and prevent segregation and premature setting.
questions.n: Slow rotation keeps the mix homogeneous and prevents the aggregates from settling to the bottom during the drive.

questions.q: For 'Massive' concrete sections, why is a very low slump (25-50 mm) preferred?
o: To minimize the internal temperature rise caused by hydration.
To make the concrete lighter.
Because mass concrete doesn't need strength.
To make it easier for the workers to shovel.
questions.n: Less water in the mix helps control the thermal expansion and cracking common in large-volume pours.

questions.q: In a 'Designed Mixture,' who typically specifies the 'slump' and 'strength' requirements?
o: The Structural Engineer/Architect.
The Truck Driver.
The Local Building Department.
The Concrete Supplier.
questions.n: The design professionals determine the required performance standards that the mix must meet.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a 'Fine Aggregate' in a concrete mix?
o: River Sand.
Crushed Gravel.
Steel Rebar.
Cement Paste.
questions.n: Sand is the primary fine aggregate used to fill the voids between larger gravel stones.

questions.q: Why is the 28-day mark used as the 'Full Strength' benchmark for concrete?
o: Because concrete stops hardening after 28 days.
It is an industry standard that allows enough time for the majority of the chemical hydration to complete.
It aligns with the typical billing cycle of construction projects.
Because it takes 28 days for the water to evaporate.
questions.n: At 28 days, concrete has achieved the vast majority of its potential strength, making it the legal and technical baseline.

questions.q: What is the minimum concrete cover required for reinforcement in concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth?
o: 50 mm
75 mm
40 mm
20 mm
questions.n: Direct contact with soil requires a thicker protective layer to prevent corrosion from ground moisture and chemicals.

questions.q: When concrete is vibrated too much during placement, it results in 'Segregation.' What exactly is occurring?
o: The concrete becomes too hot.
The coarse aggregate settles to the bottom while the fines and water rise.
The air bubbles become too large.
The cement paste hardens too quickly.
questions.n: Over-vibration causes heavier stones to sink, leaving a weak, water-rich layer at the top.

questions.q: Which specific test is used to measure the consistency of very dry, low-slump concrete commonly used in roller-compacted projects?
o: Compression Test
Kelly Ball Test
Vebe Consistometer Test
Slump Test
questions.n: This test uses vibration to determine how long it takes for a dry mix to consolidate, which is more accurate for stiff concrete.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of 'Tie Bars' in concrete pavement construction?
o: To prevent the concrete from freezing.
To allow the slabs to move independently.
To hold adjacent slabs together and prevent the opening of longitudinal joints.
To increase the compressive strength of the concrete.
questions.n: Deformed tie bars ensure that the two slabs act as a single unit laterally.

questions.q: In the 'Standard Penetration' (Kelly Ball) test, what is the weight of the metal ball used?
o: 50 lbs
10 lbs
30 lbs
20 lbs
questions.n: The standard Kelly Ball is a 30-pound hemisphere that is dropped into the fresh concrete.

questions.q: What is 'Crazing' on a concrete surface?
o: A network of fine, shallow cracks forming a hexagonal pattern.
The chemical reaction between aggregates and cement.
Large cracks that go through the entire slab.
The process of smooth-finishing the surface with a trowel.
questions.n: Crazing is a surface defect caused by the top layer drying much faster than the bottom.

questions.q: Which concrete additive is specifically designed to reduce the surface tension of the mix water, making it 'wetter'?
o: Superplasticizer
Silica Fume
Calcium Chloride
Fly Ash
questions.n: By reducing surface tension, superplasticizers allow for high workability with very low water content.

questions.q: What is the standard size of a concrete cylinder used for compressive strength testing in the Philippines (and under ACI)?
o: 150 mm x 300 mm
50 mm x 50 mm
200 mm x 400 mm
100 mm x 200 mm
questions.n: The 6x12 inch (150x300mm) cylinder is the universal standard for strength testing.

questions.q: In the context of reinforcement, what is a 'Chair'?
o: A seat for the inspector during the pour.
A device used to support rebar and maintain its proper distance from the formwork.
The base plate for a steel column.
A tool used for bending steel bars.
questions.n: Chairs ensure that the steel remains at the correct 'cover' depth during the concrete pour.

questions.q: Which type of cement is known as 'Moderate Sulfate Resistant' cement?
o: Type V
Type II
Type I
Type III

questions.q: What is the risk of pouring concrete into formwork from a height of more than 1.5 meters (5 feet)?

The concrete will dry before hitting the bottom.

questions.q: In 'Post-Tensioned' concrete, when are the steel tendons usually stressed?
o: Just before the building is occupied.
After the concrete has reached a specified strength on-site.
At the 28-day mark exactly.
Before the concrete is poured.

questions.q: What does 'Honeycombing' indicate in a finished concrete wall?
o: The presence of bees on the construction site.
Voids left in the concrete due to failure of the mortar to fill spaces between aggregates.
A beautiful architectural texture.
The concrete was mixed with honey.
questions.n: Usually caused by poor vibration or congested rebar, honeycombing leaves the aggregate exposed.

questions.q: Which part of the building is most likely to use 'Lightweight Concrete'?
o: Floor toppings or roof deck insulation layers.
Retaining walls.
Main structural columns.
Heavy machine foundations.
questions.n: Lightweight concrete reduces the 'dead load' on the overall structure in non-critical load paths.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Dowel Bars' in a concrete slab joint?
o: To transfer loads across the joint while allowing for thermal expansion.
To add color to the joint.
To prevent the slab from expanding.
To act as a moisture barrier.

questions.q: Which ASTM/PNS Type of cement would be used for a project that needs to be finished extremely quickly, like a road repair?
o: Type III
Type IV
Type I
Type II
questions.n: Type III is 'High-Early Strength' cement, achieving 7-day strength in as little as 3 days.

questions.q: What is the result of 'Bleeding' in concrete?
o: It prevents the concrete from cracking.
The concrete becomes stronger.
The concrete turns red.
Water rises to the surface as the solids settle.
questions.n: Excess water moves upward, which can create a weak, dusty surface layer called 'Laitance'.

questions.q: What is the standard angle of a 'L-hook' or '90-degree hook' in rebar fabrication?
o: 135 degrees
90 degrees
180 degrees
45 degrees
questions.n: An L-hook is named after its shape, which involves a right-angle bend.

questions.q: Why is 'Saltwater' generally prohibited for use in structural concrete mixing?
o: It makes the concrete too heavy.
It makes the concrete taste bad.
Chlorides in the water will cause rapid corrosion of the steel reinforcement.
It prevents the concrete from ever setting.
questions.n: Salt promotes the 'rusting' of the internal steel, which eventually expands and cracks the concrete.

questions.q: What is 'Cold Joint' in concrete construction?
o: A joint filled with ice to keep the building cool.
A decorative groove cut into a sidewalk.
A joint designed to allow for winter expansion.
A line formed when a new batch of concrete is poured against one that has already started to set.
questions.n: The two layers do not bond properly, creating a weak point and a visible line.

questions.q: In the context of 'Shotcrete' (pneumatically applied concrete), what is the primary difference between the 'Dry-Mix' and 'Wet-Mix' processes?
o: In the dry-mix process, water is added at the nozzle rather than in the mixer.
Dry-mix requires a larger air compressor.
The dry-mix process uses smaller aggregate sizes.
Wet-mix is only used for vertical surfaces.
questions.n: Dry-mix allows the operator to control water content instantly at the point of application, whereas wet-mix is pre-hydrated.

questions.q: What is the primary architectural benefit of using 'Pervious Concrete' in a parking lot design?
o: It stays cooler in the summer due to its light color.
It is cheaper to install because it uses less cement.
It reduces stormwater runoff by allowing water to pass directly through the slab.
It has a higher compressive strength than standard concrete.
questions.n: Pervious concrete eliminates fine aggregates to create a network of voids for ground-water recharge.

questions.q: When analyzing the 'Bond' between concrete and rebar, which feature of the rebar is most responsible for preventing slippage?
o: The deformations (ribs) on the surface of the bar.
The circular shape of the bar.
The chemical coating on the steel.
The weight of the steel.

questions.q: In extreme hot-weather concreting, which of the following is a common practice to keep the mix temperature below the maximum limit?
o: Adding more cement to speed up the finish.
Decreasing the mixing time.
Using dark-colored aggregate.
Replacing part of the mixing water with shaved ice.
questions.n: The latent heat of fusion in ice is highly effective at lowering the temperature of the fresh mix.

questions.q: What is the specific danger of 'Thermal Cracking' in mass concrete pours like bridge piers or dam sections?
o: It causes the concrete to turn into a liquid state.
It prevents the rebar from bonding.
The temperature difference between the hot core and the cooler surface creates tensile stresses.
The outside of the concrete stays too hot.
questions.n: As the core expands and the surface contracts, the concrete exceeds its tensile capacity and cracks.

questions.q: Which document is used on-site to track the specific location of every concrete truck's pour and its associated test cylinders?

Pour Log (or Concrete Placement Log)
Bill of Materials
Structural Calculation Sheet

questions.q: What is 'Self-Consolidating Concrete' (SCC) and why is it used in complex architectural forms?
o: Concrete that hardens without any cement.
Concrete that expands to fill the forms.
Concrete that uses only fine sand.
A highly flowable mix that can fill congested forms without mechanical vibration.

ASTM C150
ASTM D1751

questions.q: What is the primary function of 'Steam Curing' in a precast concrete plant?
o: To accelerate the gain of strength so forms can be reused within 24 hours.
To change the color of the concrete to white.
To make the concrete waterproof.
To keep the concrete clean.

To make it easier for the workers to reach.

questions.q: What is a 'Waterstop' and where is it installed?
o: A flexible strip of PVC or rubber cast into joints to prevent water passage.
A chemical spray for the surface of a slab.
A type of umbrella for construction workers.
A valve in the plumbing system.
questions.n: Waterstops are placed across construction or expansion joints in basements, tanks, and pools.

questions.q: Why is 'Over-troweling' a concrete surface considered a defect?
o: It makes the surface too smooth and slippery.
It draws too much fine material and water to the surface, causing it to scale or dust.
It makes the concrete dry out too fast.

No. 32 (1-inch) rebar

questions.q: In a 'Standard 28-day Compression Test,' if the cylinder fails by cracking in a well-defined cone shape at both ends, what does this tell the lab technician?

The test was valid and the loading was uniform.
The testing machine was broken.

questions.n: Cone failure (Type 1) is the standard expected failure mode for a properly capped and centered cylinder.

questions.q: What is 'Formwork Pressure' and why must an architect/engineer be concerned with the rate of pour?
o: The lateral hydraulic force exerted by liquid concrete against the vertical forms.
The weight of the workers standing on the forms.
The pressure of the air inside the form.
The suction force when removing the forms.
questions.n: If concrete is poured too fast, the liquid 'head' height increases, which can burst the forms.

questions.q: When specifyng 'Exposed Aggregate' finish, which chemical is often sprayed on the formwork or fresh surface to prevent the top 'skin' from hardening?
o: Curing Compound
Surface Retarder
Accelerator
Acid Wash
questions.n: By delaying the set of the very top layer, the paste can be washed away later to reveal the stones.

questions.q: Which type of 'Admixture' would you specify for a concrete tank that must be used to store potable (drinking) water?
o: High-Early Strength Accelerator
Lead-based stabilizer
Oil-based plasticizer
Crystalline Waterproofing Admixture
questions.n: These react with moisture to grow crystals that plug capillaries, making the concrete itself the water barrier.

questions.q: What is 'Creep' in concrete structures?
o: The movement of workers on a site.
Cracks caused by tree roots.
The sudden collapse of a building.
The long-term deformation of concrete under a sustained constant load.
questions.n: Concrete will continue to slowly compress or sag over years if it is constantly supporting a heavy weight.

questions.q: In a 'Pre-tensioned' concrete member, when is the tension typically released to transfer the stress to the concrete?
o: Immediately after the concrete is poured while it is still liquid.
After the concrete has reached a specific compressive strength.
Before the concrete is poured into the forms.
28 days after the pour, regardless of strength.
questions.n: The bond between the hardened concrete and the steel allows the compressive force to be transferred once the jacks are released.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of 'Stirrups' in a reinforced concrete beam?
o: To carry the longitudinal tension loads.
To make the beam look thicker.
To resist diagonal tension (shear) stresses.
To provide a surface for the concrete to stick to.
questions.n: Stirrups are vertical or inclined reinforcements designed to prevent diagonal cracking near the supports.

questions.q: Which specific admixture is most commonly used to produce 'Heavyweight Concrete' for radiation shielding in hospitals?
o: Expanded Shale
Silica Fume
Fly Ash
Barite or Magnetite Aggregates
questions.n: High-density minerals like barite are used as aggregates to increase the mass per unit volume for blocking X-rays and gamma rays.

questions.q: In a 'Two-Way Slab' system, what is the function of a 'Drop Panel'?
o: To reduce the amount of concrete needed for the slab.
To resist 'punching shear' and reduce the negative moment at the column support.
To provide a space for electrical conduits.
To act as a decorative ceiling element.
questions.n: Thickening the slab around the column provides more area to resist the heavy shear forces concentrated there.

questions.q: What does the term 'Efflorescence' refer to on a finished concrete or masonry surface?
o: The growth of moss and algae in damp conditions.
The process of the concrete turning into sand.
White, powdery salt deposits left on the surface as water evaporates.
A type of high-gloss paint used for concrete.
questions.n: Soluble salts are carried by moisture to the surface; when the water dries, the salts remain.

questions.q: In the context of concrete curing, what is the 'Heat of Hydration'?
o: The boiling point of concrete.
The thermal energy released by the chemical reaction between cement and water.
The heat applied to the forms in winter.
The temperature of the water used in the mix.
questions.n: The hydration of cement is an exothermic process, meaning it generates heat as it sets.

questions.q: Which tool is used immediately after pouring to strike off excess concrete and bring the top surface to the proper grade?
o: Bull Float
Screed (or Straightedge)
Edger
Steel Trowel
questions.n: Screeding involves moving a long straight board back and forth to level the wet concrete.

questions.q: What is 'Polymer-Modified Concrete' and why might it be used in a renovation project?
o: Concrete that can be melted and reshaped.
Concrete mixed with plastic beads for decoration.
Concrete using latex or resins to improve adhesion and tensile strength in thin patches.
Concrete that is 100% made of recycled plastic.
questions.n: The polymers act as a secondary glue, making it excellent for thin overlays and repairs where standard concrete would peel off.

questions.q: Which type of joint is specifically designed to allow for the horizontal movement of concrete slabs due to thermal expansion and contraction?
o: Contraction Joint (Control Joint)
Construction Joint
Cold Joint
Isolation Joint (or Expansion Joint)
questions.n: These joints are filled with compressible material to allow the slab to grow and shrink without crushing adjacent structures.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the standard diameter for a #10 reinforcing bar?
o: 32 mm
1 inch
10 mm
1.25 inches
questions.n: In the metric system used in the Philippines, rebar sizes are designated by their diameter in millimeters.

questions.q: What is 'Spalling' in a concrete structure?
o: The process of painting the concrete.
The vertical alignment of a column.
The chipping or breaking away of the concrete surface, often exposing rebar.
The mixing of sand and gravel.
questions.n: Internal pressure (like rusting rebar) pushes the outer 'shell' of concrete off in chunks.

questions.q: Why is 'Silica Fume' added to a concrete mix for high-performance applications?
o: To make the concrete set faster in the rain.
To create a very dense, high-strength concrete with extremely low permeability.
To give the concrete a blue color.
To make the concrete cheaper.
questions.n: The microscopic particles fill the tiny voids between cement grains, creating a much tighter matrix.

questions.q: When casting 'Architectural Concrete' with a smooth finish, what type of form release agent should be avoided?
o: Used engine oil or dirty grease.
Chemically active agents.
Non-staining mineral oils.
Water-based emulsions.
questions.n: Waste oils will stain the concrete permanently and can interfere with the bond of future paints or sealers.

questions.q: What is the primary architectural purpose of a 'Broom Finish' on a sidewalk?
o: To hide cracks in the slab.
To create a slip-resistant texture for pedestrians.
To make the concrete dry faster.
To remove dust from the surface.
questions.n: The tiny ridges created by the broom provide traction, especially when the surface is wet.

questions.q: Which property of concrete is measured by the 'Cylinder Split-Tensile Test'?
o: Abrasion Resistance
Flexural Strength
Tensile Strength
Compressive Strength
questions.n: By loading a cylinder on its side, the lab can calculate the indirect tensile capacity of the concrete.

questions.q: What is the 'Water-Cement Ratio' and how does it generally affect concrete quality?
o: It only affects the color of the concrete.
It measures the amount of water in the gravel.
Lower ratio generally leads to higher strength and durability.
Higher ratio means stronger concrete.
questions.n: Using only enough water for hydration results in a denser, less porous, and stronger final product.

questions.q: In 'Post-Tensioned' slabs, what is the purpose of the 'Anchorage' at the end of the tendons?
o: To lock the tension into the cables and transfer the compressive force to the slab edge.
To connect the slab to the plumbing pipes.
To keep the tendons from rusting.
To provide a lifting point for a crane.
questions.n: After the hydraulic jacks pull the cables, the anchor 'bites' the steel to hold the stress permanently.

questions.q: What is a 'Flying Form' system in high-rise construction?
o: Large, prefabricated floor formwork modules that are moved from floor to floor by a crane.
Forms made of lightweight paper.
A type of drone used to inspect concrete.
Forms that are thrown away after use.
questions.n: This system speeds up construction by allowing entire floor sections to be 'flown' up to the next level.

questions.q: Which type of cement is specifically designed for use in massive structures like dams to prevent cracking from internal heat?
o: Type V (Sulfate Resistant)
Type III (High-Early Strength)
Type I (Normal)
Type IV (Low Heat of Hydration)
questions.n: Type IV slows down the chemical reaction, spreading the heat release over a longer period to reduce thermal stress.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of 'Segregation' during the vibratory compaction of concrete?
o: The gravel sinks to the bottom while water and cement paste rise, creating weak layers.
The concrete will turn a different color.
The concrete will set too fast.
The rebar will melt.
questions.n: Excessive vibration causes the heavy stones to settle, leaving the top of the pour structurally inferior.

questions.q: In the context of 'Prestressed Concrete,' what is the primary difference between 'Pre-tensioning' and 'Post-tensioning' regarding the bond with concrete?
o: There is no difference in the bond; both rely entirely on end-anchorages.
In pre-tensioning, the steel is bonded to the concrete throughout its length; in post-tensioning, it is often unbonded or grouted later.
Pre-tensioning only uses circular wires, while post-tensioning only uses flat plates.
Post-tensioning is done in a factory, while pre-tensioning is always done at the construction site.
questions.n: Pre-tensioning relies on the direct bond formed as the concrete hardens around the already-stretched strands, while post-tensioning happens in ducts.

questions.q: What is the primary reason for using 'Epoxy-Coated Rebar' in structures like bridges or coastal condominiums?
o: To help the concrete flow better around the bars.
To increase the tensile strength of the steel.
To make the rebar easier to weld on-site.
To provide a barrier against chloride-induced corrosion.
questions.n: The epoxy prevents salt and moisture from reaching the steel surface, which is critical in marine or de-icing environments.

questions.q: When using 'High-Range Water Reducers' (Superplasticizers), what is the most significant benefit provided to a 'Designed Mixture'?
o: It allows for a significantly lower water-cement ratio while maintaining high workability.
It eliminates the need for any curing period.
It changes the color of the concrete to a brighter white.
It makes the concrete lighter in weight.
questions.n: This allows for the creation of high-strength concrete that can still flow easily into dense reinforcement.

questions.q: Which type of 'Construction Joint' is typically used in large floor slabs to prevent the concrete from cracking randomly due to drying shrinkage?
o: Expansion Joint
Cold Joint
Isolation Joint
Contraction (Control) Joint
questions.n: These are weakened planes (often saw-cut) that encourage the concrete to crack in a neat, straight line.

questions.q: What is the standard purpose of 'Vapor Barriers' placed beneath concrete slabs-on-ground?
o: To provide a cushion for the slab to move on.
To prevent moisture from the soil from migrating through the slab and damaging floor finishes.
To keep the concrete from drying out too quickly from the bottom.
To increase the compressive strength of the slab.
questions.n: It blocks capillary action and water vapor that could cause delamination of tiles or mold in carpets.

questions.q: What is 'Laitance' on a concrete surface and why is it a problem for further construction?
o: A chemical that speeds up the setting time.
A weak layer of cement and fine particles that prevents the bond of subsequent toppings.
A layer of decorative pebbles.
The vertical alignment of the formwork.
questions.n: It forms when excess water bleeds to the surface; it must be removed before applying new concrete or coatings.

questions.q: Which of the following is the primary purpose of 'Skin Reinforcement' in deep concrete beams (beams with a height greater than 900mm)?
o: To make the beam easier to transport.
To increase the total load-carrying capacity of the beam.
To control cracking in the side faces of the beam.
To provide a surface for attaching architectural cladding.
questions.n: In very deep beams, the concrete on the sides can crack between the main steel and the neutral axis; skin steel keeps these cracks small.

questions.q: Which method of concrete curing is most effective in preventing 'Plastic Shrinkage Cracks' during extremely windy and dry conditions?
o: Using liquid membrane-forming curing compounds.
Removing the formwork earlier.
Fogging (applying a fine mist of water) or using windbreaks.
Adding more cement to the mix.
questions.n: Fogging keeps the surface humidity high, preventing the rapid evaporation that causes plastic shrinkage.

questions.q: What is the function of 'Fly Ash' when used as a partial replacement for Portland cement?
o: It increases the water demand of the mix.
It improves workability and reduces the heat of hydration.
It is used to make the concrete more flammable.
It makes the concrete reach its full strength in only 3 days.
questions.n: The spherical shape of fly ash particles acts like 'ball bearings,' making the mix easier to pump and reducing heat in mass pours.

questions.q: In architectural concrete, what is 'Bush-hammering' used for?
o: To compact the concrete inside the forms.
To drive the rebar deeper into the slab.
To create a textured, rough surface by removing the smooth outer skin of the hardened concrete.
To polish the surface to a mirror-like shine.
questions.n: It uses a mechanical tool with a 'toothed' head to pit the surface and expose the aggregate.

questions.q: What is the primary danger of using 'Aggregates' that contain reactive silica in a concrete mix?
o: The concrete will catch fire.
It can lead to 'Alkali-Silica Reaction' (ASR), causing internal expansion and 'map cracking'.
It makes the concrete too heavy to lift.
The concrete will not harden at all.
questions.n: A gel forms and absorbs water, swelling inside the concrete and literally tearing it apart from the inside out.

questions.q: Which reinforcing bar grade is standard for structural elements in the Philippines requiring a yield strength of 415 MPa (60,000 psi)?
o: Grade 40
Grade 80
Grade 60
Grade 33
questions.n: Grade 60 is the most common structural grade for beams and columns in modern reinforced concrete design.

questions.q: When using 'Welded Wire Fabric' (WWF), what do the numbers in a designation like '6x6 - W1.4xW1.4' represent?
o: The height and width of the building.
The spacing of the wires (6 inches) and the cross-sectional area of the wires.
The number of workers needed to carry the roll.
The temperature at which the mesh melts.
questions.n: The first two numbers indicate the mesh grid size, while 'W' numbers indicate wire gauge/size.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Grouting' in a bonded post-tensioned system?
o: To protect the tendons from corrosion and ensure the bond between the steel and the concrete.
To increase the weight of the slab.
To act as a lubricant for the cables.
To make the outside of the building look better.
questions.n: Filling the duct with cement grout locks the tendon to the structure and keeps out moisture.

questions.q: In concrete slab construction, what is the 'Bleed Water'?
o: Water that turns the concrete red.
Water that is trapped inside the gravel.
Water used to clean the tools.
Excess mixing water that rises to the surface as the heavier aggregates settle.
questions.n: It is a natural part of the consolidation process, but finishing too early can trap it under the surface.

questions.q: What is 'Formwork Shoring' and why is it critical in multi-story construction?
o: Temporary vertical supports used to hold the weight of freshly poured concrete until it gains strength.
A type of insurance for concrete workers.
It is the process of painting the plywood forms.
The metal ties that hold the wall forms together.
questions.n: Without shoring, the wet concrete and construction loads would collapse the newly cast floor.

questions.q: Why is 'Curing' particularly critical for concrete made with 'Silica Fume'?
o: Silica fume makes the concrete too cold to set.
It actually needs less curing than normal concrete.
Because silica fume will dissolve in the rain.
Because silica fume concrete has very little bleed water, making it highly susceptible to surface drying.
questions.n: With no 'upward' moisture to replace what evaporates, the surface can crack almost immediately if not kept moist.

questions.q: What is the standard purpose of 'Spiral Reinforcement' in a circular concrete column?
o: To make the column easier to build.
To save on the amount of steel used.
To act as a lightning rod for the building.
To provide continuous lateral confinement, greatly increasing the ductility and load capacity of the column.
questions.n: The spiral 'hoop' prevents the concrete core from bursting outward under heavy vertical loads.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the common commercial length for standard reinforcing steel bars?
o: 20 feet and 40 feet only.
6 meters, 7.5 meters, 9 meters, 10.5 meters, and 12 meters.
Any length you want, up to 100 meters.
3 meters and 4.5 meters
questions.n: Standard metric lengths in 1.5-meter increments are provided by local mills to minimize wastage on site.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the standard yield strength of a Grade 40 reinforcing bar in Metric units?
o: 275 MPa
500 MPa
415 MPa
230 MPa
questions.n: This value corresponds to the yield strength of Grade 40 steel commonly used for low-rise residential structures.

questions.q: Which specific type of cement is designated as 'High Sulfate Resistant' and is ideal for structures in direct contact with severe groundwater or seawater?
o: Type V
Type I
Type IV
Type II
questions.n: This designation is specifically formulated to withstand severe sulfate action from soil or water.

questions.q: What is the minimum concrete cover for a reinforced concrete beam that is NOT exposed to earth or weather?
o: 75 mm
50 mm
40 mm
20 mm
questions.n: Standard building codes specify this distance for beams and columns to protect rebar from fire and corrosion.

questions.q: In the 'Nominal Mix' method, a 1 : 2 : 4 ratio is most likely to produce which compressive strength after 28 days?
questions.n: This is the characteristic strength expected from a standard Class A mix under normal conditions.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of adding 'Silica Fume' to a high-performance concrete mix?
o: To increase the setting time
To decrease permeability and increase strength
To reduce the density of the concrete
To provide entrained air bubbles
questions.n: The extremely fine particles create a 'packer effect' that makes the concrete nearly watertight and much stronger.

questions.q: Which test is used to determine the consistency and workability of concrete by measuring the diameter of the spread of a concrete sample?
o: Air Content Test
Slump Test
Flow Table Test
Cylinder Test
questions.n: This test is specifically used for high-workability or self-leveling concrete to measure how far it spreads.

questions.q: What is the standard weight of one bag of Portland Cement in the Philippines?
o: 40 kg
50 kg
45 kg
25 kg
questions.n: This is the standard unit weight for a single bag of cement used in site-mixing calculations in the Philippines.

questions.q: In a reinforced concrete slab, 'Temperature Bars' are placed in which direction?
o: Only in the middle third of the slab
At a 45-degree angle
Perpendicular to the main reinforcement
Parallel to the main reinforcement
questions.n: These bars are designed to resist cracks caused by expansion and contraction in the direction where main steel is absent.

questions.q: Which defect is characterized by the separation of the top layer of a concrete slab from the main body, often due to finishing while bleed water is still present?
o: Delamination
Scaling
Efflorescence
Honeycombing
questions.n: This occurs when air or water is trapped under a prematurely densified surface, causing the top 'skin' to peel away.

questions.q: What is the 'Initial Set' of concrete?
o: The moment water is first added to the cement
The time when concrete reaches 50% of its strength
The time when formwork can be safely removed
The point when concrete can no longer be mixed or vibrated effectively
questions.n: This marks the transition from a plastic state to a rigid state where further work would damage the internal structure.
